purpose: Review the primary stomach-content findings for Johnius borneensis in Hegde's Goa University thesis. Preserve the study locality, methods and %FO interpretation; do not present the result as Philippine or Caraga diet evidence.

studySource.author: Mahabaleshwar R. Hegde
studySource.title: Studies on spatio-temporal variation and community structure of demersal resources of Goa, west coast of India
studySource.workType: Doctor of Philosophy thesis in Marine Sciences
studySource.institution: Goa University, Department of Marine Sciences
studySource.dietChapter: Chapter 7, Trophic dynamics and diet overlapping of sciaenids, pp. 69-79
studySource.studyArea: Demersal fish surveys in Goa, west coast of India, including bay-estuarine and offshore coastal waters; the thesis describes bottom trawling down to 20 m depth.
studySource.samplingPeriod: January 2009 through December 2011 for the broader survey.
studySource.sampleScope: The thesis reports 1,284 stomachs across 10 sciaenid species in its diet chapter. The species-specific Johnius borneensis denominator could not be reliably recovered from the text-extracted table, so no count is asserted here.

method.procedure: The thesis describes removing and weighing the whole gut, preserving it in 70% alcohol, examining stomach contents gravimetrically, identifying prey to the lowest possible taxon, and recording frequency of occurrence. Unrecognizable digested contents and decompression-affected stomachs were excluded.
method.reportedMetric: % frequency of occurrence (%FO) for sciaenids, selected by the author because planktonic prey could make volume-to-weight conversion problematic.
method.metricMeaning: The source defines %FO as the percentage of non-empty stomachs in which a prey item occurred; it is not percentage of diet mass or percentage of fish biomass.

dietEvidence.studyLocality: Goa, west coast of India; not the Philippines.
dietEvidence.sourceNarrativeSummary: The thesis states that J. borneensis preferred zooplankton, reporting 78.36 %FO, and describes it as a zooplanktivore with mysis and prawn larvae among the cited prey. It reports broader size-related variation in sciaenid diets, but the text-extracted species table's column alignment was not visually verified, so no species-specific size-class breakdown or exact per-species sample denominator is recorded.
dietEvidence.interpretation: This is direct diet evidence for the Goa study population only. It is a stronger method source than a generalized species account but cannot resolve Agusan prey without a Philippine study.

accessAndReuse.fullTextAccess: University repository PDF text was inspected through the web document viewer. Direct visual screenshot of the diet table was unavailable; the table's header/value alignment was therefore treated as unresolved.
accessAndReuse.license: No explicit open license or reuse terms were verified for the thesis.
accessAndReuse.decision: Retain a concise attributed research paraphrase and link. Do not reproduce the table, figure or substantial thesis text; public or commercial Bangwit reuse remains unapproved.

limitations: Goa, India is outside the Philippines; the diet result cannot be assigned to Caraga, Pagatpatan, or any Philippine waterbody.
The thesis-wide 1,284 stomach count covers 10 sciaenid species; species-specific Johnius borneensis stomach count was not reliably parsed and is intentionally omitted.
The reported 78.36 is %FO, not percent by weight, percent of individual fish, or an angling success rate.
Prey items and feeding patterns may vary with size, habitat, season, and local prey availability.
The text-extracted table alignment could not be visually verified, so no table-derived size-group result is asserted.
No thesis license, public app permission, current occurrence, legal catchability, safety conclusion, or bait guidance was established.
nextAction: Keep Goa as a comparative-only diet source. Continue the Caraga freshwater evidence queue with an independently documented river/lake fish survey, and search local stomach-content research separately for each priority species rather than generalizing this result.

references.supports: Thesis identity, Goa study scope and period, stomach methods, %FO definition, species-level narrative statement and unresolved table extraction.
Prior step 342 secondary Western Central Pacific species account; retained separately from the primary Goa study.
